title: Struct Basics
concept: A bundle that groups multiple variables together (user-defined type)

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
This header is needed to use `printf`.

This lesson covers struct definition, member access, and copy behavior.

steps.title: Defining the struct 'blueprint'
steps.explanation:
`struct Point { int x; int y; };` is a blueprint for a new type with two members.

This step is a type definition -- no actual variable memory is created yet.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

Next we will create struct variables to observe values and copy behavior.

steps.title: Declaring and initializing a struct variable
steps.explanation:
`struct Point p1 = {10, 20};` creates the actual variable `p1` and initializes its members.

A single variable name can manage a bundle of related data.

steps.title: Accessing and printing struct members
steps.explanation: The dot operator (`.`) accesses `p1.x` and `p1.y` to read values.

steps.title: Copying a struct (value copy)
steps.explanation:
The `p2 = p1` assignment copies the member values to a new variable.

The original and the copy exist independently afterward.

steps.title: Modifying the copied struct member
steps.explanation: Changing a member of the copy `p2` only affects the copy.

steps.title: Verifying the original (p1)
steps.explanation:
Checking the original value confirms it remains unchanged.

This is key evidence that it was a value copy.

steps.title: Verifying the copy (p2)
steps.explanation: The copy retains the modified value and is separate from the original.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation:
The program ends with `return 0;`.

Key point: Struct assignment is a value copy, and member access uses the `.` operator.

quiz.question: What operator is used to access struct members?
quiz.explanation:
When accessing members from the variable itself, use the dot (`.`).
When using a pointer, use the arrow (`->`).

misconceptions.wrong: A struct's size equals the sum of its members' sizes
misconceptions.correct: Usually true, but it can be larger due to padding.
misconceptions.why: The CPU inserts empty spaces (padding) between members to read data faster (Memory Alignment).

keyTakeaway: Group related data with `struct`. Using `=` copies the entire value.
